claims.text: Rapid or low-temperature synthesis of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanomaterials results in partial atomic mixing and local elemental segregation.
Thermal annealing within an optimized temperature and time window enables full entropic mixing.
Thermal annealing produces a more homogeneous distribution of noble metals in a high-entropy alloy.
A homogeneous elemental distribution creates a higher density of uniformly active catalytic sites.
The increased density of uniformly active sites improves catalytic activity.
Annealing-induced homogeneous mixing improves catalyst stability relative to minimal annealing.
The annealing temperature must be high enough to activate atomic diffusion.
Annealing above the suitable process window causes particle coalescence, sintering, or undesired grain growth.
Reliable material formation is characterized by negligible elemental segregation and formation of a single-phase solid solution.
Enhanced thermal energy during annealing increases atomic diffusion and mixing.
Annealing reduces local diffusion barriers that would otherwise cause elemental segregation.
A homogeneous elemental distribution stabilizes the Gibbs free energy of the alloy.
Homogeneous mixing facilitates the formation of coordination-unsaturated catalytic sites.
Coordination-unsaturated sites regulate electronic structure and enhance catalyst–substrate interactions, thereby improving catalytic performance.
Annealed material will exhibit a more uniform elemental distribution in high-resolution EDS mapping than minimally annealed material.
Annealed material will contain fewer secondary phases than minimally annealed material.
Annealed material will have a higher turnover frequency or reaction rate than minimally annealed material.
Minimally annealed, partially segregated material has less reliable and lower catalytic performance.
The proposed relationship may fail when dopants such as nitrogen or extreme composition changes dominate structural ordering.
